text.p: Base metal prices drifted lower on the LME and gold closed weaker in New York but wheat prices rose on bullish USDA reports. Oil and sugar prices also weakened.
The CRB index closed 1.15 points down at 240.83.
The base metals drifted steadily lower on the London Metal Exchange on Tuesday after the market got spooked by firmer levels reached early in the day, traders said.
Copper failed a halfhearted attempt to hurdle tenacious resistance at $2,290 while aluminium lost its grip on eight-month highs and zinc edged back from fresh 23-month high levels.
Traders said the drift lower occured amid thin volumes and did not seriously impact the recent upside momentum.
"People got too bullish at the highs. This is a normal correction from there," one trader said.
On the downside, if copper managed to breach key support towards $2,230, then a move below $2,200 was likely.
However, interim support around $2,250 was generally expected to hold in the near term.
Three-months copper finished the kerb down $15 at $2,255 after hitting an early high of $2,280. A rise in LME stocks of 4,725 tonnes was expected but neverthless put a damper on the upside.

However, nearby spreads remained firm. Cash to threes backwardation edged up from Monday's levels to end at around $235. Traders noted that the February dates remained extremely tight, and some voiced concern about whether the tightness would be rolled forward.

Aluminium, boosted by a surprise stocks drop of 6,525 tonnes, initially charged to an eight-month high of $1,640. But, forward selling swiftly emerged to erode its gains, and copper's weakness also heped drag it lower.
It last traded at $1,618, down $6 from Monday's close.

Zinc similarly eased back from a fresh 23-month high achieved early on when LME stocks were reported to have dropped by 2,000 tonnes. It finished the kerb at $1,138, down $16 from Monday and off from Tuesday's high of $1,157.
Nickel followed the trend lower, finishing the day $50 down at $7,300, while lead was $11.50 lower at $713.

New York precious metals futures gave back early gains to end mostly lower Tuesday, as the U.S. dollar remained firm and US equity markets saw new record highs. "Precious metals still look mostly oversold but still refuse to bounce much and it was a sloppy close," said Anthony Raia of Linnco Futures Group in Chicago. US Federal Reserve chairman Greenspan gave Congress an upbeat assessment of the US economy, allowing US bond markets to recover ground and the stock market to push higher, meaning paper assets retained their attraction, analysts said.
COMEX February gold saw a session high at $356.30 early, but ended down 80 cents at $353.80, not far from the contract low at $352.60 seen on January 15.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $352.70/20, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $354.70 and the New York close Monday at $353.30/80.

"While prices continue to hold above key support at $350, renewed short selling cannot be ruled out in this highly technical trading environment," CPM Group analyst Edward Kempf said. Gold prices are now down to a level that may mean some gold producers are struggling to break even, analysts said.
CBOT wheat futures closed higher on bullish input from USDA's weekly export inspections plus aggressive buying by key commercial Cargill Inc, traders said.

USDA early Tuesday said U.S. wheat inspected for export during the week ended January 16 totaled 14.334 million bushels. The tally was above the 12.111 million bushels reported inspected the previous week and above trade expectations which ranged from eight million to 13 million bushels.
Wheat closed unchanged to 5-1/4 cents per bushel higher, with March up 4-3/4 at $3.82-1/4 a bushel.

NYMEX crude oil futures closed lower as heating oil extended its losses for the fourth consecutive session, as ample supply and mild weather had dealers unwinding positions. February crude oil fell 43 cents to $24.80 a barrel.

A late bout of mixed selling pressured March CSCE world sugar futures to close at a 10-month low. The spot month ended down 0.18 cent at 10.17 cents a lb, its lowest since March 8. The rest shed 0.19 to 0.08 cent. Merrill Lynch said in a daily sugar report that some increase in physical offtake is likely at current levels. However, it "should not be sufficient to spark a strong move back up," the report said.
